title: A Big Reason Teachers Struggle With Classroom Management https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2023/02/28/teachers-struggling-classroom-management/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Drawing on years of coaching struggling teachers, Linsin identifies a single root cause behind much classroom management difficulty: teachers simply don't know exactly what they want from students in each moment, leaving 'gray areas' that students inevitably fill with disruptive choices of their own. He argues it is less about which specific policy a teacher picks and more about the act of deciding clearly and then teaching and enforcing that decision consistently. His prescribed method for closing gray areas is visualization: sitting quietly with pencil and notepad, picturing the optimal version of a routine or transition in vivid detail, writing down exactly what it looks like, and treating that vision as the standard to teach and model. He frames this as an ongoing process, to be repeated whenever new gray areas surface through renewed uncertainty and misbehavior.
points: Many classroom management struggles trace back to teachers not knowing precisely what they want from students moment to moment.
Undefined 'gray areas' get filled by students with disruptive choices when expectations aren't explicit.
It matters less which specific policy is chosen than that a clear decision is made and consistently taught and enforced.
The recommended method is visualization: picturing the optimal version of a routine in detail and writing it down as the standard.
The process should be repeated whenever new gray areas surface through renewed misbehavior.
quotes: I know this to be true after years of working with thousands of teachers struggling with classroom management:
It’s when students don’t know what is expected that problems arise. These are called gray areas. And you must eliminate them.
In which case, they will make their own—and almost always disruptive—choice.
Grab a pencil and notepad and find a comfortable place to sit. Close your eyes and watch in your mind’s eye as your students perform whatever unanswered questions you have in the most optimal way.

When and if new gray areas are exposed, through your uncertainty and subsequent misbehavior, then repeat the process. Visualize. Write it down. Then teach and model until there is no doubt what you want.
